t: A Simple, Effective Homework Plan For Teachers: Part 1 https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/07/31/effective-homework-plan-for-teachers-part-1/
q: Dealing with homework can be the source of great stress for teachers; it’s a rare week that I don’t receive at least one email asking for advice.

The skills needed to complete the evening’s homework must be thoroughly taught during the school day. If your students can’t prove to you that they’re able to do the work without assistance, then you shouldn’t assign it.
You should tell parents at back-to-school night, “I got it covered. If ever your child doesn’t understand the homework, it’s on me. Just send me a note and I’ll take care of it.
Is there anyone, for any reason, who will not be able to turn in their homework in the morning? I want to know now rather than find out about it in the morning.
If you see more than this, then you know your lesson was less than effective, and you’ll have to reteach.
The personal leverage you carry–that critical trusting rapport you have with your students–combined with the always lurking peer pressure is a powerful force.

t: A Classroom Management Strategy For The First Days Of School -of-school/
q: The beginning of the school year is the perfect time to send a pleasant behavioral shock wave through your new class of students and their parents.

Some teachers recommend creating a classroom management plan with student input. The reasoning being that if students are involved in making the rules, they’ll have ownership and be more likely to behave. Hogwash.
You’re the authority in the classroom. You set the tone. You make the rules. Therefore your classroom management plan should be prepared and included in this packet.
Detailed modeling and role-play are most effective for teaching your plan, policies, and routines. Again, let students experience the ins and outs of each one before sharing them with parents.
It’s much more difficult to manage a classroom that’s already out of control–like putting toothpaste back in the tube.
The classroom management-only packet is a great way to do this. It gets students and parents on board and on record within the first few days of school.

Keeping your cool and letting your classroom management plan do its job, however, will put you in stark contrast with most of your colleagues, and your students will love and respect you because of it.
Solving problems and addressing areas of concern shows students, perhaps more than anything else, that you really care.
Master the art of meaningful praise. Small, personal, sincere acts of praise can have a profound impact on students and is especially effective in endearing them to you.
Be worthy of a hero’s status by carrying yourself with calm confidence. Be decisive, prepared, and behave in manner you expect from them.

t: 7 Classroom Management Strategies To Get Your Class Back On Track
q: Whatever it is, there are times when your class just can’t seem to get it together. They’re unfocused, squirrelly, prone to misbehavior.
Take your students outside or to the school gym, line them up on the end line of the basketball court, and run.
Have your students grab their backpacks, jackets, and lunches, walk them outside the classroom, and start your day over again.
Use the one-minute of silence strategy followed by belly breathing. This sends oxygen to the brain, lowers blood pressure, and calms the mind.
Don’t give your students an explanation of why you’re using any of these back-on-track classroom management strategies. Don’t lecture them or tell them how awful they are. Just do it.
With experience, you’ll get a feel for what your students need and when, and you’ll be able to dial it up in a hurry.

t: Why A Letter Home Is An Effective Consequence https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/07/03/why-a-letter-home-is-an-effective-consequence/
q: I can’t emphasize enough that consequences for misbehavior are only a small part of classroom management. By themselves, they cannot deter students from misbehaving.
A form letter—official looking and impersonal—strikes the right tone in communicating the seriousness of breaking rules and interrupting learning.
If you don’t get the letter back the next day, simply follow up with a phone call. Chances are you’re being tested.
If a child breaks your classroom rules three times in one day, his or her parents have a right to know.
They’re accountable to you because they must get the letter signed and returned—honoring and respecting your authority.
And they’re accountable to themselves—understanding that there are consequences for the choices they make.
